summary.text: An S wave, or shear wave, is one of the two main kinds of elastic body wave, moving through the body of an object rather than along its surface.
It is transverse: particles move at right angles to the wave's direction under shear stress, so it cannot cross gases or liquids of very low viscosity.
Because S waves cannot pass through Earth's molten outer core, they leave a shadow zone on the side opposite their origin.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Second wave type a seismograph detects

facts.label: Medical use
facts.value: Magnetic resonance elastography of living tissue

items.prompt: In one kind of seismic wave, the ground moves at right angles to the direction the wave travels. Which wave is that?

options.label: A P wave
A sound wave in air
An S wave
A compression wave

items.explain: S waves are transverse: particle movement is perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

items.prompt: Why can an S wave not travel across a still pond of water?

options.label: Water is too dense for waves
Runny water cannot resist being sheared
Water soaks up all vibration
The pond is too shallow

items.explain: An S wave's restoring force comes from shear stress, so it cannot propagate in liquids of zero or very low viscosity.

items.prompt: S waves cannot cross Earth's molten outer core, yet S waves do travel through the solid inner core. How do they get there?

options.label: They slip through cracks in the outer core
The inner core makes its own quakes
They curve around the core through the mantle
P waves turn into S waves at the inner core's edge

items.explain: When a P wave strikes the boundary between the molten and solid cores at an angle, S waves form and travel through the solid inner core.

items.prompt: A seismograph records a P wave and then, a little later, an S wave from the same quake. Why does the S wave show up later?

options.label: It travels more slowly through solid rock
It starts some time after the quake
It must loop around the core
It is only made near the surface

items.explain: S waves are the second type of wave detected because they travel more slowly in solids than P waves.

items.prompt: Doctors want to know how stiff a patient's liver is without cutting into it. How does magnetic resonance elastography do this?

options.label: It passes X-rays through the organ
It sends shear waves in and images them by MRI
It heats the tissue and tracks warming
It tests a blood sample for stiffness

items.explain: A vibrator sends shear waves into the tissue, MRI views the response, and the measured wave speed and wavelength give properties such as the shear modulus.

items.prompt: A material's shear stiffness rises while its density stays the same. What happens to the speed of S waves through it?

options.label: It drops to zero
It falls
It rises
It stays exactly the same

items.explain: S-wave speed is β = √(μ/ρ), so a larger shear modulus μ with the same density ρ gives a faster wave.
